recipe.history:
Short ribs are one of the oldest and most beloved cuts of beef in the culinary canon, with roots stretching back centuries across Europe and Asia. In Korea, galbi — flanken-cut short ribs — have been braised and grilled since at least the Joseon Dynasty, marinated in soy, sesame, and pear. In France, the côte de bœuf braisée emerged from peasant kitchens where tough, collagen-rich cuts were coaxed into tenderness over long, slow fires. The short rib, taken from the lower portion of the rib cage, is richly marbled with intramuscular fat and dense connective tissue — qualities that make it almost worthless at high heat and absolutely transcendent when braised low and slow. Pearl onions, meanwhile, have graced European tables since the Romans; their small, sweet bulbs were pickled and preserved across France, Germany, and England as a way of extending the harvest and brightening the richness of slow-cooked meats. Horseradish, fiery and pungent, has been cultivated since antiquity in Eastern Europe, particularly in Poland, Ukraine, and the Jewish Ashkenazi tradition, where it appears as chrain — grated horseradish mixed with beet or vinegar — and served at Passover Seders as a symbol of bitterness. Together, these ingredients form a portrait of hearty, cold-weather comfort food that has fed families across centuries and continents.

Braised short ribs made their way into American cuisine through the great waves of immigration in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Eastern European and Jewish immigrants brought their traditions of slow-braised beef with root vegetables, onions, and vinegary condiments to cities like New York and Chicago, where pot roast became a Sunday institution. The Irish and German immigrants who settled the Midwest carried similar traditions — slow-cooked beef with onions and potatoes — that became the backbone of American home cooking. By the mid-20th century, braised beef had been elevated from peasant food to restaurant fare, and by the 1990s and 2000s, chefs like Daniel Boulud and Tom Colicchio were placing slow-braised short ribs on white tablecloths. It was only a matter of time before someone put them on a bun. The short rib burger became a mark of the gourmet burger movement of the 2000s and 2010s — a way of honoring the burger's blue-collar roots while elevating it with technique and time. Pickled pearl onions added brightness; creamy horseradish cut through the fat. The potato roll, soft and pillowy, was the final grandfatherly touch.

I remember the first time I truly understood what a braised short rib could do. I was twelve years old, sitting in my grandfather's kitchen on a gray November Saturday, and the whole house smelled like something ancient and warm. He had started the braise the night before — beef short ribs in a Dutch oven with red wine, beef stock, thyme, bay leaves, and a whole mess of pearl onions he'd peeled himself, one by one, at the kitchen table while watching the evening news. By morning the meat had collapsed off the bone into thick, ropy, magnificent strands. He shredded it with two forks, reduced the braising liquid until it was glossy and almost syrupy, and folded it all back together. Then — and this is the part I still think about — he slapped it all onto a soft potato roll he'd picked up from the bakery that morning, smeared with horseradish cream, and handed it to me without a word. It was the best thing I had ever eaten. I've been chasing that feeling ever since, and every time I make this burger I am twelve years old again, sitting at that linoleum table with the window fogging up from the steam.

There is a philosophy at the heart of great cooking that this burger embodies, and it applies just as much to the patty as to everything else: respect the ingredient enough to cook it properly. For a beef patty — which, unlike the braised short rib, is cooked to order — that means medium rare, every single time. Medium rare, 130–135°F internal temperature, is the only temperature at which a beef patty achieves its full potential. Below that and you risk the texture being too soft and the fat not fully rendered; above that and you begin to lose the moisture, the tenderness, the pink blush that tells you the proteins haven't been over-tightened. I know there are people who will argue for medium, and I know there are well-meaning food safety guidelines, and I respect both — but I also know what I taste. A patty cooked to medium rare still has juice that runs when you press it, fat that coats your lips, and a flavor that is unmistakably, unapologetically beef. Cook it past that and you are eating something else entirely. This burger, with its fall-apart braised short rib and its properly cooked patty, deserves nothing less than that commitment.
ingredients: 1 cup mashed russet potato (about 1 large potato), cooled
3½ cups all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
1 bottle (750 ml) dry red wine (Cabernet Sauvignon or Côtes du Rhône)
1 lb pearl onions, peeled (blanch 30 seconds to slip skins)
Fresh watercress or baby arugula, for garnish
instructions: 1. Make the pickled pearl onions (ideally 24–48 hours ahead): Bring a pot of water to a boil. Score an X in the root end of each pearl onion and blanch for 30 seconds. Transfer to an ice bath, then slip off the skins. Combine vinegar, water, sugar, salt, peppercorns, mustard seeds, and thyme in a small saucepan and bring to a boil, stirring to dissolve. Pack peeled onions into a clean jar, pour hot brine over them, cool to room temperature, then refrigerate for at least 4 hours and up to 2 weeks.

2. Braise the short ribs (best done the day before): Preheat oven to 325°F. Pat short ribs completely dry with paper towels and season generously on all sides with kosher salt and black pepper. Heat oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Sear ribs in batches, 3–4 minutes per side, until deep mahogany brown. Do not crowd the pan. Remove ribs and set aside.

3. Pour off all but 2 tbsp of fat from the Dutch oven. Add onion, carrots, and celery and cook over medium heat, stirring occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until softened and beginning to caramelize. Add garlic and cook 1 minute more. Add tomato paste and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes until it darkens slightly.

4. Pour in the red wine and scrape up any browned bits from the bottom of the pot. Bring to a boil and reduce by half, about 10 minutes. Add beef stock, thyme, bay leaves, and rosemary. Return ribs to the pot — they should be mostly submerged. Bring to a bare simmer, cover tightly, and transfer to the oven.

5. Braise for 3 to 3½ hours, until the meat is completely fork-tender and falling from the bone. Remove ribs from the liquid and let cool slightly. Strain the braising liquid, discarding solids, and return it to the pot. Simmer over medium-high heat until reduced by half and sauce-like in consistency, about 20 minutes. Shred the rib meat, discarding bones and any large fat pieces, and fold the meat back into the reduced braising liquid. Season to taste with salt and pepper. Refrigerate overnight if making ahead; the fat will solidify and can be skimmed.

6. Make the potato rolls: Dissolve yeast in warm milk with 1 tbsp sugar. Let stand 5–10 minutes until foamy. In a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook, combine flour, remaining sugar, and salt. Add the yeast mixture, mashed potato, softened butter, and eggs. Mix on low until a shaggy dough forms, then increase to medium and knead for 8–10 minutes until smooth, soft, and slightly tacky.

7. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise in a warm place for 1–1½ hours until doubled in size. Turn out onto a lightly floured surface, divide into 8 equal portions, and shape each into a smooth ball. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing 2 inches apart. Cover with a damp kitchen towel and let rise 45 minutes until puffed.
8. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush rolls with egg wash (yolk + milk). Bake 18–22 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool on a wire rack before slicing.

9. Make the creamy horseradish sauce: Combine sour cream, horseradish, mayonnaise, white wine vinegar, Dijon, salt, and white pepper in a bowl. Whisk until smooth. Fold in chives. Taste and adjust horseradish and salt as needed. Refrigerate until serving.

10. Form the burger patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 6 oz each). Gently form each into a patty approximately ¾ inch thick. Make a shallow dimple in the center of each patty with your thumb to prevent doming during cooking. Season both sides generously with salt, pepper, and garlic powder just before cooking.

11. Cook the patties: Heat a cast iron skillet or griddle over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3–4 minutes on the first side without pressing. Flip once. Add butter and thyme sprigs to the pan. Tilt the pan and baste the patties with the foaming butter for 1–2 minutes. Cook to an internal temperature of 130–135°F for medium rare. Remove from heat and rest 3 minutes.
12. Toast the buns: Melt butter in a skillet over medium heat. Place rolls cut-side down and toast until golden and crisp, 2–3 minutes.
13. Warm the braised short rib mixture gently in a saucepan over medium-low heat, adding a splash of beef stock if needed to loosen it.

14. Assemble: Spread a generous layer of creamy horseradish sauce on the cut side of both the top and bottom bun. Place the medium rare patty on the bottom bun. Pile a generous heap of warm braised short rib over the patty. Top with 6–8 pickled pearl onions, halved. Add a small handful of watercress or arugula. Crown with the top bun. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Serve immediately.
